items.title: The Essential-Body Verses Open: Avoid All Evil, Abandon All Desire

items.zh: 「應發勤精進，常堅固勇猛，恒修不放逸，五支善安住」者，此頌顯示由被甲、方便、無退精進故，修習五支不放逸故，令所修學清淨殊勝。五支不放逸者，謂去、來、今、先時所作，及俱所行。「當隱自諸善，亦發露眾惡。得諸衣服等，麁、妙皆歡喜。少隨於世務，麁弊亦隨轉。受杜多功德，為寂離煩惱」者，此二頌中，顯示遠離眷屬貪欲多欲不知足因故，及遠離多欲不知足障淨學因故，學得清淨。「當具足威儀，應量而攝受，終無有所為，詐現威儀相」者，此頌顯示具足威儀故；不於他前詭現相故；凡所攝受善知量故；為修梵行，資持壽命有所受故；學得清淨。「不自說實德，亦不令他說，雖有所方求，而非現異相。從他邊乞求，終不強威逼，以法而獲得，得已不輕毀」者，此二頌中，顯示遠離綺言說故，詭現相故，強威逼故，以所得利轉招利故，令所修學清淨殊勝。「不耽著利養，及所有恭敬，亦不執諸見，增益與損減」者，此頌顯示不耽著利養恭敬故，不執著五種惡見故，令所修學清淨殊勝。「不著順世間，無義文呪術；亦不樂畜積，無義長衣鉢」者，此頌顯示不執著諸惡見因，外道邪論，以能障礙取蘊解脫。彼所制造，名順世間。及遠離耽著利養恭敬因，長衣鉢等。因清淨故，學得清淨。「恐增諸煩惱，不染習居家，為淨修智慧，當親近賢聖」者，此頌顯示遠離所治因，親近能治因故，學得清淨。「不畜朋友家，恐發憂悲亂，能生苦煩惱，纔起尋遠離」者，此頌顯示若親近居家，生憂悲散亂，增長諸煩惱，能為眾苦因。由親近彼能生眾苦，煩惱纔生尋即除遣，如是顯示對治之因。「不受於信施，恐加害瘡皰，於如來正法，甞無有棄捨」者，此頌顯示不貪著利養恭敬，不堅執諸惡邪見，不虛受用信施，不毀謗正法，亦能遠離貪著後世諸欲，及能生起諸惡見因。如是所學清淨殊勝。「於他愆犯中，無功用、安樂，常省自過失，知已速發露」者，此頌顯示遠離作意求覓他人所有過失；於自善品無有散亂常生歡喜；於自過失如實了知，發露悔除，離增上慢；由此因緣學得清淨。「若犯於所犯，當如法出離，所應營事中，能勇勵自作」者，此頌顯示出離所犯，及能遠離貪受他人恭奉侍衛，由此因緣學得清淨。「於佛及弟子，威德與言教，一切皆信受，觀大罪、不謗」者，此頌顯示信圓滿故，於能誹謗見大罪故，學得清淨。「於極甚深法，不可思度處，能捨舊師宗，不堅執自見」者，此頌顯示遠離安住自見取故，清淨殊勝。
items.en: 'One should arouse diligent effort, always firm and courageous, constantly cultivate heedfulness, and abide well in its five limbs': this verse shows that, through armour-like, applied, and unflagging effort, and through cultivating the five limbs of heedfulness, what is trained becomes pure and excellent. The five limbs of heedfulness concern the past, the future, the present, what was done before, and what is practised together. 'One should hide one's own good deeds and also disclose one's faults; whatever robes and the like one receives, coarse or fine, be glad of them all; be little involved in worldly affairs and get by with what is poor; take up the qualities of the austerities, for calm and freedom from afflictions': these two verses show that the training becomes pure because one leaves behind the causes of desire for followers, of many wants, and of discontent, and leaves behind the causes by which many wants and discontent obstruct pure training. 'One should be complete in deportment, accept things in due measure, and never put on a show of deportment': this verse shows that the training becomes pure because one is complete in deportment; does not put on a false show before others; knows well the measure of whatever one accepts; and accepts things to sustain one's life in order to practise the holy life. 'Do not speak of your own real virtues, nor have others speak of them; though you seek something, do not make a show of special signs; when begging from others, never use force or pressure; obtain things by the Dharma, and having obtained them, do not disparage them': these two verses show that what is trained becomes pure and excellent because one leaves behind flattering talk, false shows, force and pressure, and using what one has gained to attract further gain. 'Do not be attached to gain and respect, and do not cling to views that add or take away': this verse shows that what is trained becomes pure and excellent because one is not attached to gain and respect and does not cling to the five kinds of bad view. 'Do not cling to the worldly-minded, meaningless texts and spells, nor delight in hoarding meaningless spare robes and bowls': this verse shows not clinging to the causes of bad views, the wrong treatises of non-Buddhists, because they obstruct liberation from the aggregates of grasping; what those people compose is called 'worldly-minded'. It also shows leaving behind spare robes, bowls, and the like, which are causes of attachment to gain and respect. Because the causes are pure, the training becomes pure. 'Fearing to increase the afflictions, do not become attached to household life; to purify and cultivate wisdom, keep company with the wise and noble': this verse shows that the training becomes pure because one leaves behind the causes of what is to be counteracted and keeps company with the causes of what counteracts. 'Do not keep households as friends, fearing they will stir up sorrow, grief, and distraction, which give rise to suffering and afflictions; as soon as these arise, leave them behind at once': this verse shows that keeping company with households produces sorrow, grief, and distraction, increases the afflictions, and becomes a cause of many sufferings. Since keeping company with them produces many sufferings, as soon as an affliction arises one dispels it at once; this shows the cause of the counteraction. 'Do not accept the offerings of the faithful, fearing they will harm you like a festering sore; never abandon the Tathāgata's true Dharma': this verse shows not being greedy for gain and respect, not clinging firmly to bad wrong views, not using the offerings of the faithful in vain, and not slandering the true Dharma; and also being able to leave behind attachment to the sense pleasures of later lives, which can give rise to bad views. In this way what is trained becomes pure and excellent. 'Make no effort over others' faults, and be at ease; always examine your own faults, and having recognised them, quickly confess them': this verse shows leaving behind the intention to seek out other people's faults; being undistracted in one's own wholesome qualities and always glad; knowing one's own faults as they are, confessing and repenting of them, and being free from overestimation. For these reasons the training becomes pure. 'If you commit an offence, make amends for it in accordance with the Dharma; in whatever tasks should be done, be energetic and do them yourself': this verse shows making amends for offences and being able to leave behind greed for others' service and attendance. For these reasons the training becomes pure. 'In the Buddha and his disciples, their majesty and their teaching, have faith in all of it; see the great wrong and do not slander': this verse shows that the training becomes pure because faith is complete and because one sees great wrong in slandering. 'In the most profound dharmas, in what cannot be fathomed by thought, be able to give up the doctrines of your old teachers and do not cling firmly to your own views': this verse shows purity and excellence through leaving behind abiding in clinging to one's own views.

blocks.text: Fascicle 17 opens by continuing the prose commentary on the verses about precepts that you read on Day 133. **None of today's Chinese is in Ru-Yi's translation** (Ru-Yi's fascicle 17 begins at 0370a09), so the English column gives our own translation, marked as ours. The commentary also summarises it verse by verse. Keep Day 133's verses in mind as you read.

items: **Diligence.** "Rouse diligent effort, ever firm and courageous": three kinds of diligence, armour-like resolve, applied effort, and effort that does not retreat. "Heedfulness with five supports": heedfulness regarding the past, the future, the present, what was done before, and what is done together.
**Hiding one's good, disclosing one's faults.** These two verses remove the causes of craving for followers, of wanting much and never being content.

**Deportment and measure.** Full deportment, never putting on a show of dignity before others, knowing the right measure in what one receives, and accepting things only to sustain life for the holy life.
**No flattery, no pressure.** Not praising one's own virtues or having others do so; not hinting at what one wants; never pressing donors; not using what one has received to attract more.

**Gain, honour, views.** Not attached to gain and honour; not holding the five wrong views. "Worldly ways" (順世間) are the teachings of non-Buddhist schools, which obstruct liberation from the aggregates of clinging; superfluous robes and bowls feed the craving for gain.
**Households.** Not mixing with lay households, which breed sorrow and distraction; drawing near to the wise instead.
**Offerings.** Not consuming faithful offerings carelessly, "fearing to aggravate the wound", and never abandoning the true Dharma.
**Others' faults and one's own.** Not looking for others' faults; rejoicing in one's own good; knowing one's own faults as they are, confessing them, and so freeing oneself from arrogance.
**Release and responsibility.** Making amends for any offence; doing one's own tasks rather than enjoying others' service.
**Faith.** Full faith in the Buddha and his disciples; seeing great wrong in slandering them.
**Letting go of one's former school.** Regarding the deepest teachings, giving up "one's old teacher's doctrine" and not clinging to one's own views.

blocks.text: Each verse ends with the same refrain in the prose: "thus training becomes pure". Purity here is not a single act but a hundred small habits: what one accepts, how one speaks, where one goes, how one handles a fault. The last verse is striking: even attachment to one's own prior teachers' views is a fault to be let go.

quiz.q: According to the prose, what are the "five supports" of heedfulness?
options: Heedfulness regarding the past, the future, the present, what was done before, and what is done together
The five faculties of faith, effort, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom
The five places a monastic should avoid
quiz.why: The prose glosses 五支不放逸 as heedfulness regarding the past, future, present, what was done before, and what is done together (去、來、今、先時所作，及俱所行).

quiz.q: Why does the prose say a renunciant should hide their own good qualities and disclose their faults?
options: To deceive donors into giving more
To remove the causes of craving for followers and of wanting much without contentment
Because the Vinaya forbids speaking of virtue at all
quiz.why: The prose says these two verses show freedom from the causes of craving for a following and of wanting much and never being content.

quiz.q: What does "worldly ways" (順世間) refer to in the verse "not attached to worldly ways, to pointless writings or incantations"?
options: The teachings of non-Buddhist schools, which obstruct liberation
quiz.why: The prose explains 順世間 as what the non-Buddhists' wrong treatises produce, which obstruct liberation from the aggregates of clinging.
